newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn coalition strikes income tax compromise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn coalition strikes income tax compromise.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition has struck a deal to cut income taxes under a major tax reform intended to take effect by 1999, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday.
Speaking as he entered a marathon final meeting of a tax working group, Waigel said the new rates would create "a real incentive for new jobs" for Germany's unemployment-hit economy.

Waigel did not give details, but sources from the policy group said a compromise model had been agreed between Waigel's wish to keep Germany's sliding tax scale and the call by junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP) for a low entry rate.
The new tax model would start with a flat rate of 15 percent on annual income of between 13,000 ($8,000) and 20,000 marks.
The rate would then jump to 22 percent and rise in a to a top rate of 39 percent.
The new tax model would cut income taxes sharply from today's entry rate of 26 percent and top rate of 53 percent.
The FDP's chief tax negotiator Hermann Otto Solms told reporters that the goal of the reforms was to offer tax relief to low wage-earners.
The tax reform, at the centre of damaging coalition wrangling over recent months, is likely to become the centrepiece of Kohl's bid next year for a record fifth general election victory.
Government leaders want the lower income tax rates to boost job creation after unemployment hit a post-war record of over 4.1 million, seasonally adjusted, in December.
High unemployment, which results in a drag on tax revenues and extra welfare costs, is seen as a threat to efforts to cut borrowing and qualify this year for European monetary union.

Those fears received fresh impetus in a new official report which predicted an unemployment rate of 11 percent this year -- a figure equivalent to 4.2 million jobless which is 200,000 higher than the view on which Waigel based his 1997 budget.

The tax policy group was due to finalise its work by Wednesday evening. Chancellor Helmut Kohl will chair a meeting of chiefs from his three-party coalition on Thursday to set the seal on the tax package.
In addition to the income tax cuts, corporation taxes would fall to 35 percent from 47 percent now. The corporate tax changes will take effect from the start of 1998.
Meanwhile, a slew of tax breaks would be abolished to make the German tax system more simple and effective. Waigel has said that taxpayers would be 25 billion marks better off at the end of the day.
Waigel said the question of raising the 15 percent rate of value-added tax to help offset the cuts in direct taxation was still open after a coalition meeting on Wednesday morning.
The issue of value-added tax has also prompted tensions in the coalition.

Waigel wants to raise VAT by one point, but a group of regional officials in Kohl's Christian Democrat party (CDU) flatly oppose a hike. Other coalition officials want a bigger VAT rise to bale out the social security system.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) say they would veto a VAT increase, if it was used to finance income tax cuts, through their majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.
"The government should not promise tax cuts on one side and take the money out people's pockets on the other," SPD tax spokesman Joachim Poss told the Boerse Online newspaper.

Although the main points of the reform should be clear by Thursday, more discussions will be needed before legislation is finalised, CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said on Tuesday. ($1=1.6223 Mark)
